2.0.s.en: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

2.0.0.en: 1 My son, if you come to serve the Lord God, stand fast in righteousness and godliness, and prepare your soul for temptation. 2 Direct your heart and endure. Incline your ear and receive the words of reason, and make not haste in time of calamity. 3 Wait patiently for what you wait for from God; cleave to Him and do not turn aside, that you may be increased in life at your latter end. 4 Whatever comes upon you, accept it, and be patient in the changes of your lowly estate, 5 for gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation. 6 Believe in Him, and He will help you. Order your ways aright and hope in Him. Keep His fear, and abide in it until your old age.

2.0.1.en: My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation [1].

2.0.2.en: The word son (or child), teknon, occurs 36 times in this book.

2.0.3.en: "My son": Sirach regards his school as a family that has its role in the life of society. So he calls his disciples "his sons," at times in the plural, a sign of the unity of the disciples with one another and of his relation to them as a father, and at times he speaks in the singular, "my son," to bring out the personal side of each one of them. Sirach wishes to walk in the spirit of God, who deals with the community, whether leaders or people, as all being the people of God, the object of His special love and care. At the same time he sees in each son a particular member who has his own place in his father's heart.

2.0.4.en: Sirach presents two complementary ideas: that wisdom shows itself in the service of the Lord, and also that it is impossible to attain wisdom without long-suffering in temptations. These two ideas never leave Sirach's thought.

2.0.5.en: The subject of "temptations" in the life of the young must be discussed, for it is fitting for the young man to learn in some detail not only about the blessings promised to those who strive to please the Lord, but also to know that temptations accompany him during his striving. He must know beforehand what may befall him. This is what the Apostle James affirmed in his epistle: "Behold, we count them happy which endure. You have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy" (Jas 5:11), referring to what befell righteous Job.

2.0.6.en: After the wise man has linked wisdom with obedience to the divine commandment and the enjoyment of the fear of the Lord, he assures us that the way of God's wisdom exposes us to temptations. Truly the cost of the way is many troubles, but it brings with it surpassing blessings (Sir 4:17-18; 6:24-31).

2.0.7.en: The Lord did not hide this truth from us, but said to His disciples: "Go your ways: behold, I send you forth as lambs among wolves" (Lk 10:3). He also said: "But before all these, they shall lay their hands on you, and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues, and into prisons, being brought before kings and rulers for My name's sake. And it shall turn to you for a testimony... And you shall be betrayed... and some of you shall they cause to be put to death. And you shall be hated of all men for My name's sake" (Lk 21:12-13, 16-17). And the Apostle James says: "My brethren, count it all joy when you fall into divers temptations; knowing this, that the trying of your faith works patience" (Jas 1:2-3). It was also said: "Fear none of those things which you shall suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that you may be tried; and you shall have tribulation ten days" (Rev 2:10).

2.0.8.en: In the days of Ben Sirach, opposition to faith in God was centered on the spread of Hellenistic paganism, which crept even into the temple in Jerusalem and reached its height in the days of Antiochus Epiphanes (the antichrist of the Old Testament). Whoever wished to abandon Hellenism while holding fast to the Law exposed himself to persecution by the Greek rulers.

2.0.9.en: For the believer these temptations perform a work of purification, just as fire refines gold (Prov 17:3). Trust in God's promises, moreover, brings us into divine help in the midst of affliction (Ps 37:3-6; Prov 3:5-6).

2.0.10.en: What the Fathers of the Church wish to affirm is that the temptations that God permits to come upon believers do not mean God's anger against them or vengeance upon them, but are a sign of divine love, for their purification and progress and for crowning them with the crown of victory. And if He is angry with them, His anger springs from His fatherly love for them.

2.0.11.en: v It is clear that You are angry, truly angry as a father who corrects, and not as a judge who condemns [1].

2.0.12.en: v Those whom God appointed before the foundation of the world to take the image of His only-begotten Son (Rom 8:29), who in particular was pressed in His sufferings as the great cluster of grapes, were, before they drew near to the service of God, enjoying in the world a kind of sweet freedom, like clusters of grapes or olives hanging on the tree. But as it was said: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" (cf. Sir 2:1).

2.0.13.en: Everyone who draws near to the service of God finds himself in a winepress; he endures troubles, and is crushed and pressed, not to perish in this world, but to flow into the storehouses of God.

2.1.0.en: The coverings of fleshly lusts are removed from him, like the skin of the grape (when it is pressed)... The Apostle speaks of it: "Put off the old man... and put on the new man" (Col 3:9-10; Eph 4:22). All this is accomplished only by pressing. For this reason the churches of God in this time are called "winepresses" [2].

2.1.1.en: v Be patient and bear the trials that you meet on your way to reach God, for He receives with thanks those who endure patiently in affliction...

2.2.0.en: The fire of temptations and difficulties produces men who are strong in faith; it may be painful, but it brings forth the strong, because they rest upon a strong foundation [3].

2.2.1.en: St. Augustine v (A letter of consolation to a father whose two daughters died, and also his maidservant)

2.2.2.en: I do not deceive you with flattering words, nor do I pull the ground from under your feet with fawning praise. Rather I say what is good for you to hear: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" (Sir 2:1). "When you shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do" (Lk 17:10).

2.3.0.en: Say to God: "The two daughters whom You have taken from me are Your gift. The maidservant whom You have taken for Yourself You also lent me for a time for my comfort. I am not grieved that You have taken them back; rather I thank You that You gave them to me before" [4].

2.4.0.en: v It must be noted that if the Lord had not begun by fasting, Satan would not have found the opportunity (to tempt Him), according to the saying: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" (Sir 2:1). The Savior's own answer indicates that He was tempted as a man: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God" (Mt 4:4). Therefore, if anyone does not feed on the word of God, he does not live [5].

2.5.0.en: St. Jerome v Those who have chosen to live a glorious and blameless life must store up beforehand in their mind sufficient zeal to accomplish it. And let them remember him who said: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure" (Sir 2:1-2). But those who have no such zeal, how can they reach the goal set before them? The Lord says: "Or what king, going to make war against another king, sits not down first, and consults whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that comes against him with twenty thousand?" (Lk 14:31) [6]

2.5.1.en: v Any matter that happens unexpectedly and is grave drives even the brave to disturbance, and sometimes to unbearable terrors. But if it is mentioned beforehand that it will happen, then expecting it lightens the weight of its attack, and this, I believe, is the meaning of the phrase "I was prepared, and was not troubled."

2.6.0.en: For this reason the divinely inspired Scripture says to those who seek glory through their holy conduct: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure" (Sir 1:2). And it does not speak so as to produce in men laziness and indifference... For this reason the Savior of all prepared the disciples beforehand, telling them that He would suffer on the Cross and die in the body once He reached Jerusalem [7].

2.6.1.en: St. Cyril of Alexandria v When the soul begins to love heavenly realities, and fixes herself strongly on this essential peace, then the ancient enemy, who fell from heaven (Lk 10:18), comes down feeling envy, and begins to multiply his hidden snares.

2.6.2.en: He develops temptations with greater violence than usual. He tempts all the more the soul that resists. Therefore it is written: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" [1], and be firm in justice and fear [8].

2.6.4.en: v God often directs certain kinds of threats that come upon our heads, not in order to bring them down upon us, but in order to draw us to Himself, and when we return to Him the fear quickly dissolves.

2.6.5.en: Surely, if we remained in the same state during temptations, in tranquility, there would be no need of temptations. And why do I speak of ourselves? Even the saints of old learned a great lesson, for the prophet says: "It is good for me that You have humbled me" (Ps 119:71). And Jesus also said to the apostles: "In the world you shall have tribulation" (Jn 16:33). And Paul refers to this when he says: "There was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted" (2 Cor 12:7)... If we review the whole life of David, we find that he was most glorious when he was in danger, he and those like him.

2.7.0.en: Such was the state of Job, who shone with the greatest brightness during his troubles. And Joseph also was proved in this way all the more... For all who have worn such crowns of glory gained them by troubles and temptations [9].

2.8.0.en: v Let us not grieve because of the evils that happen to us. This is soundness of mind. "And make not haste in time of trouble" (Sir 2:2). Many have their manifold sorrows at home, and we share one another's sorrows, even if not from the same source. One is unhappy because of his wife, another because of his child, or his servant, another because of his friend, another because of his enemy, another because of his relative, and another because of a loss that has befallen him. The causes of sorrow are many, so that we find no one free from some kind of toil or misery. Therefore it is fitting for us to be patient, and not to think that we alone are not happy [10].

2.9.0.en: v There is nothing in moral life that is exempt from sorrow; if not today, then tomorrow, and if not tomorrow, then some day later troubles come. Just as no one can make a long voyage by sea and feel that he is never unsettled, so it is not possible to pass through this life without experiencing sorrow; yes, even for the rich man, since he is rich he will pass through occasions that he does not desire. Yes, even the king himself, for many things govern him, and he cannot accomplish all that he ought to do [11].

2.9.1.en: v If we sin, God may raise up our enemies against us to discipline us, and therefore we ought not to fight them, but we must examine ourselves and train ourselves. And as long as He has let them loose upon us because of our sins, when we fight them He gives them victory over us. For this reason He commanded us not to repay our enemies. Let us accept trials as we accept medicines from the physician so that we may be saved, and as we accept discipline from the father so that we may be refined. Therefore the wise man said: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" (Sirach 2:1).

2.9.2.en: St. John Chrysostom Set your heart aright, and constantly endure, and make not haste in time of trouble [2].

2.9.3.en: Ben Sirach does not ignore human feelings; in time of affliction man suffers and groans, but by faith he cries out to the Lord, and He removes anxiety from him. This is what happened with the Apostle when he cried to the Lord three times to take the affliction from him, and the Lord's answer was: "My grace is sufficient for you: for My strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor 12:9).

2.9.4.en: When St. John Chrysostom suffered pains and persecution from the Empress Eudoxia, aided by the very men of the clergy, he wrote from his prison to Bishop Cyriacus:

2.9.5.en: [When I was driven out of the city I was not troubled, but said to myself: If the Empress wishes to banish me, let her do so, for "the earth is the Lord's"!

2.9.6.en: And if she wishes to saw me asunder, I have Isaiah as an example!

2.9.7.en: And if she wishes to drown me in the ocean, I think of Jonah!

2.9.8.en: And if I am cast into the fire, I find that the three youths endured this in the furnace!

2.9.9.en: If I am put before ferocious beasts, I remember Daniel in the lions' den!

2.9.10.en: If she wishes to stone me, Stephen, the first martyr, is before me!

2.9.11.en: If she asks for my head, let her do so, for the Baptist shines before me!

2.9.12.en: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I leave the world.

2.10.0.en: Paul reminds me: "If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" [12].]

2.11.0.en: And St. Cyprian wrote to some confessors, saying to them: ["In all these things we are more than conquerors through Him that loved us" [13].]

2.11.1.en: v When God wishes to give a man victory and magnify him, He first delivers him to evil (temptations) to be tested and examined, and then He shows his beauty to the world by the blessings that God works with him.

2.11.2.en: When God wished to give Joseph victory and make him lord over Egypt, what was the beginning of His work to bring him to a good end? First his brothers seized him, and insulted him, and mocked him, and stripped off his clothes, and cast him into the pit, and cut off his hope, and sold him to merchants, and he became a slave serving masters, and the handsome son of free men who had done no wrong was enslaved.

2.12.0.en: Whoever saw this evil deed could not have thought that all these evils were being done for Joseph's good. But God, who knew what He wished to do for him, had no pity on him when he groaned under the weight of all these evils, but let him fall into the pit, and be sold to merchants, and be thrust into prison unjustly. After all this his beauty shone like the sun, and his right was displayed like gold, and his evils vanished like smoke, and he mounted to the top of the chariot like a king, and rose in the greatness for which God had set him, that he might be humbled and so be exalted [14].

2.12.1.en: St. Jacob of Serugh v The truly wise man has one concern, which is to obey Almighty God with all his heart and to please Him. And he teaches one thing, only one, which is how to do, as far as he can, what is agreeable to God, thanking Him for His compassionate care, which works in everything that happens in his life.

2.13.0.en: And just as it is only fitting for us to thank physicians for treating our bodies, even if they give us bitter medicines that are unwelcome, so it is not fitting for us to be ignorant that all things work together for good, by the grace of divine providence, and so deny God's kindness in the things that seem painful to us [15].

2.14.0.en: St. Anthony the Great v Through divine providence everything is surely good and for the benefit of the soul; all that happens is for our good and our happiness, for God loves us and protects us. As the Apostle says, we must give thanks to God in everything for His goodness toward us (1 Thess 5:18). Let us not sink in our hearts nor lose heart over what happens to us, but accept events, convinced that all that God does with us proceeds from His goodness because He loves us, and all that He does is right. Truly it is impossible for things to go well except through the mercies of God [16].

2.14.1.en: Father Theodorus of Gaza v Let us drive away from us all worldly cares (anxiety) by prayer and hope. And if we cannot reach this to perfection, let us confess our weakness before God and not cease striving in prayer.

2.14.2.en: St. Mark the Ascetic Cleave to Him and do not turn aside, that you may be honored at the end of your life [3].

2.14.3.en: Ben Sirach offers us a practical experience that we benefit from in the midst of affliction, which is that we do not direct our eyes downward lest sorrow swallow us up, but look upward, or into our depths. So we hold fast to the Lord and cleave to Him, and ask for His companionship in the midst of affliction. We rejoice and sing: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ lives in me" (Gal 2:20). We enter the narrow way to see eternity cleave to us.

2.14.4.en: v We know that when a man cleaves to God, He cleanses him to lighten for him the weight of his sins, and the word of the Savior is fulfilled in him: "If you continue in My word, then are you My disciples indeed; and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free" (Jn 8:31-32). For it is God who cleanses man. And it is written that "both He that sanctifies and they who are sanctified are all of one" (Heb 11:2). And also: "Every branch in Me that bears not fruit He takes away: and every branch that bears fruit, He purges it, that it may bring forth more fruit" (Jn 2:15).

2.15.0.en: My son, cleave to God (Sir 3:2) and flee from all evil works. Help yourself, and flee from sin as one who flees from a serpent [17].

2.15.1.en: St. Stephen of Thebes v The dispensation of our God and Savior concerning man is to restore man from the fall, and to bring him back from the estrangement that came upon him because of transgression, to direct fellowship with God. Therefore Christ came in the flesh, and lived according to the pattern that we see in the Gospels, and suffered on the Cross and was buried and rose, so that man may be saved by imitating Christ and return to the ancient rank of sonship.

2.16.0.en: Likeness to Christ alone leads to the perfection of life, not only by being like Him in His life as an example of meekness and humility and patience as a pattern for our life, but also in His death. Therefore Paul, who imitated Christ, says: "That I may be conformed unto His death; if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead" (Phil 3:10-11) [18].

2.16.1.en: St. Basil the Great Whatever comes upon you, accept it, and be patient in the changes of your lowly estate [4].

2.16.2.en: Ben Sirach gives us another exercise, which is to look at the condition of mankind in the world, so that we are like one clinging to the wheel of time. The wheel turns, and we see ourselves at one time above and at another below, at one time in a certain direction and soon in the opposite direction.

2.16.3.en: The world is changing, but if we are bound to the Holy One, the wheel of time does not occupy us, but the chariot of the Cross, more radiant than the chariot of Elijah the prophet, carries us from glory to glory, until we reach the heaven that awaits us and welcomes us.

2.16.4.en: v He (the Apostle) says: "Giving thanks always for all things" (Eph 5:20).

2.16.5.en: What is this? Are we to give thanks for everything that befalls us? Yes, even if sickness or poverty befalls us. If in the Old Testament the wise man counsels us: "Whatever comes upon you, accept it, and be patient in the changes of your lowly estate" (Sir 2:4), how much more in the New Testament?!

2.16.6.en: Yes, offer thanksgivings even if you do not know the word (that you offer)!...

2.16.7.en: If you give thanks in rest and prosperity and success and wealth, this is not a great matter, nor is it wonderful; but a man needs to give thanks when he is in sorrows and afflictions and troubles. There is no better word than to say: "I thank You, O Lord"...

2.16.8.en: Let us thank the Lord for the blessings that we see and those that we do not see, and those that we receive against our will, for we receive many blessings without our wish and without our knowledge...

2.17.0.en: When we are in poverty or sickness or calamities, let us increase our thanksgivings, and I do not mean thanksgivings in words and on the tongue, but in work and deeds, and in mind and heart. Let us thank Him with all our souls, for He loves us more than our parents do, and as far as evil is from goodness, so great is the difference between God's love for us and our fathers' love [19].

2.17.1.en: St. John Chrysostom v Know that bodily illnesses are natural to the body, since it is material and corruptible. Therefore if sickness comes upon it, the soul that has learned (goodness) must take courage and endure with thanksgiving, without murmuring against God who created the body for it.

2.18.0.en: St. Anthony the Great v An elder said of poor Lazarus: "We did not see that he did any virtue, except that he never murmured against that rich man who had no mercy on him, and he was thankful to God for what he had, and for that alone God had mercy on him [20].

2.18.1.en: From the Paradise of the Fathers: for gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men (and chosen) in the furnace of humiliation [5].

2.18.2.en: If the merciful God permitted temptations beyond our power, no man would be able to stand before the cunning schemes of the evil spirits without falling to the ground. The Apostle Paul says: "But God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that you are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that you may be able to bear it" (1 Cor 10:13).

2.19.0.en: v What if we suppose that a man has fallen into sickness? Well, let him hear another counsel: "In sickness and poverty, trust in (God), for gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation" (cf. Sir 2:4-5). Therefore neither death nor loss of money nor bodily sickness, nor insult nor shame nor anything of the kind can grieve him, but makes him more joyful; what ground for sorrow, then, can there ever be? [21]

2.20.0.en: v We can say: (this) affliction makes those who are troubled more steadfast. "Tribulation works patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope makes not ashamed" (Rom 5:3-5). Do you not see that the proof that comes from affliction produces hope in the good things to come, and that steadfastness in temptations causes us hope for the future? For this reason I do not say hastily that these very afflictions point us toward the hope of the resurrection, and put those who are tempted in a better state, since he says: "For gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation" (Sir 2:5) [22].

2.20.1.en: St. John Chrysostom v Hear my prayer, O God, when I am troubled; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.

2.20.2.en: The enemies rose up against the martyrs. What was the voice of this Body of Christ (that is, the martyrs) as it prayed?

2.20.3.en: Was it praying to be delivered from the enemies, and that the enemies should have no power to kill? Were they not heard because they were killed? Did God abandon His servants who had contrite hearts, and did He despise those who had hope in Him? Surely not! For who has called upon God and been forgotten by Him? Who has trusted in Him and been left?

2.20.4.en: They were heard, and they were killed. Yet they were delivered from their enemies.

2.20.5.en: Others who were afraid yielded and lived. But these very ones were swallowed up by their enemies.

2.20.6.en: Those who were killed were saved, and those who lived were swallowed up.

2.21.0.en: This is what the voice of the recognized Psalmist pointed to when he said: "Then they had swallowed us up quick" (Ps 124:3). Many in truth were swallowed up alive, but many others were swallowed up dead. Those who count Christianity foolishness are in fact dead. There comes a time when they swallow themselves up [23].

2.21.1.en: St. Augustine Trust in Him and He will help you; order your ways aright, and put your hope in Him. [6]

2.21.2.en: The Psalmist says: "Our soul waits for the Lord: He is our help and our shield. For our heart shall rejoice in Him, because we have trusted in His holy name" (Ps 33:20-21). No one who trusts in Him is ashamed, for his soul dwells in Him, and God dwells in him (Jn 14:23). "Trust in the Lord, and do good; dwell in the land, and feed on His faithfulness... Commit your way unto the Lord; trust also in Him; and He shall bring it to pass" (Ps 37:3, 5).

2.21.3.en: v Thus thinks the soul that loves God: God is her place; and she knows no other place to dwell in, and does not dwell in any place except in God, as it is written: "Lord, You have been our dwelling place in all generations." Therefore wherever the true Christian is, he dwells in God, and God dwells in him, and he does not rely on a homeland or a place. For this reason he has no need to move from one place to a similar one. For this I beseech your love to serve your God with divine love, as you are and wherever you may be [24].

2.21.4.en: St. Jacob of Serugh v He who does not trust in God in small things reveals all the more his lack of faith in great things [25].

2.21.5.en: v "O Lord my God, in You do I put my trust" (Ps 7:1)...

2.21.6.en: Although this prayer is simple, and anyone can offer it, it was not offered here in that way. For he who places his trust in a man, or trusts in something else in life, such as authority or possessions, or anything that many regard as glorious, cannot say: "O Lord my God, in You do I put my trust."

2.21.7.en: In truth there is a commandment that it is not fitting for us to trust in rulers. "Cursed be the man that trusts in man" (Jer 17:5). Just as it is fitting for us not to worship anything besides our worship of God, so it is fitting for us not to trust in anyone other than God, the Lord of all things. It was said: "The Lord is my hope and my praise" (Ps 70:5; 118:14) [26].

2.21.8.en: v Anxiety expresses the ugliness and weakness of the soul, because of its separation from God. Let us then pray that the light of God's countenance may shine upon us. So we shall be like the saints in their meekness and peace in all circumstances, and always ready to do good, as the Psalm says: "I made haste, and was not troubled" (Ps 119:6); "You have turned for me my mourning into dancing: You have put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness" (Ps 30:11).

2.21.9.en: The joy of God does not settle in all souls, but in those souls that have wept over their sins, with many signs and continual tears, like one who has lost a loved one. Such a soul God turns from mourning into joy. The Lord of glory warns us not to be like children sitting in the market, calling to one another and saying: "We have piped unto you, and you have not danced; we have mourned to you, and you have not wept" (Lk 7:32). The pipe is a musical instrument that gives a note when it is blown, and therefore I believe that every holy prophet is a pipe in the spiritual sense, working by the breath of the Holy Spirit. It was said: "We have piped unto you, and you have not danced," and the words of prophecy urge us to work according to the commandment, which is what is called "dancing."

2.21.10.en: The prophets weep over us, and call us to weep, so that we may discover our faults in the light of their prophetic words; then we weep over our ruin and subdue our body with striving and punishment. The man who walks in such a way has his sackcloth torn and puts on the adorned wedding garment, so that he is not cast out of the wedding (Mt 22:11-13) [27].

2.21.11.en: v Question: Does he who was caught in a multitude of evils, and sinned after his baptism, fall into despair of his salvation? Or what is the measure by which a man may still continue in his hope in God's love for mankind through repentance?

2.21.12.en: Answer: If it were possible to balance God's surpassing compassion or the weight of the greatness of God's mercy against the number and weight of sins, there would be room for despair.

2.21.13.en: But if it is reasonable that the latter are subject to measure and number, while it is impossible to measure God's mercy or count His compassion, there will never be any room for despair. Rather, by knowing the mercy and condemning the sins, there is forgiveness in the blood of Christ, as it is written (Mt 26:28).

2.21.14.en: However, there are many places and ways through which we learn that we must not despair. Consider in particular the parable of our Lord Jesus Christ about the son who took his father's wealth and squandered it in sins. From the words of the Lord Himself we learn what kind of feast, and how great, befits repentance (Lk 15:22-24).

2.21.15.en: Add to this that God says by Isaiah: "Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool" (Isa 1:18). But we must know that this is fulfilled only when our repentance deserves it, if it proceeds from our hatred of sin, as it is written in the Old and New Testaments, and bears fruits worthy of it [28].

2.22.s.en: 2. He who fears the Lord is full of hope

2.22.0.en: 7 You that fear the Lord, wait for His mercy, and turn not aside, lest you fall. 8 You that fear the Lord, believe in Him, and your reward shall not be lost. 9 You that fear the Lord, hope for good things, and for everlasting joy and mercy. 10 You that fear the Lord, love Him, and your hearts shall be enlightened. 11 Look at the generations of old, and see; did ever any trust in the Lord, and was ashamed? 12 Or did any abide in His fear, and was forsaken? Or who called upon Him, and was neglected? 13 For the Lord is full of pity and mercy, forgives sins, and saves in time of affliction.

2.22.1.en: It is fitting for every man to work with all his strength, for he will not achieve what he desires while in idleness; yet what he possesses is from God, like the farmer and the fisherman, each of whom works and the Lord is the one who gives to them.

2.22.2.en: You who fear the Lord, wait for His mercy, and turn not aside, lest you fall. [7]

2.22.3.en: Remember that God's dealings through the generations build our faith and our hope on practical experience (Ps 34:8; 37:25). Let us not cast ourselves into the hands of men, but into the hands of God, for His majesty is in His mercy, and His greatness in His compassion.

2.22.4.en: v Let us learn how to endure without murmuring or objection to what happens to us, for God knows what is good for us. And we must bear calamity with thanksgiving, and then blessings will overtake us. Let us submit to everything that comes upon us, giving thanks to God for everything, for He knows what is good for us better than we know. And He loves us more than father and mother. Let these considerations be a song that we sing to ourselves in time of affliction, so that we may drive out despair and glorify God in everything [29].

2.23.0.en: St. John Chrysostom You who fear the Lord, believe in Him, and your reward shall not be lost. [8]

2.24.0.en: You who fear the Lord, hope for good things and everlasting joy and mercy. [9]

2.24.1.en: The monk Theodore was a friend of St. John Chrysostom in the ascetic life, but the beauty of a young woman of fair appearance named Hermoine led him astray, and he fell in love with her and wished to marry her. Theodore the ascetic fell in love with this woman, but his greatest fall was centered in his despair of God's accepting him and of the possibility of his returning to his former ascetic life. Prayers were offered for him and efforts were made, and finally St. John Chrysostom sent him two letters, which recorded for us the most wonderful remedy that a despairing soul needs, through living hope. They revealed to us God's unlimited mercies and His arms always open to receive sinners and fornicators, however great their sins, with a warning against the most hideous devil, namely the devil of despair.

2.24.2.en: v Do not despair of your being changed completely.

2.24.3.en: If Satan has this power, to cast you down to the ground from a towering height and lofty virtue to the utmost limits of evil, how much more is God able to raise you to your former confidence, and make you not only as you were, but happier than before [30].

2.24.4.en: v Great is the power of hope in the Lord: an unconquerable fortress, a protecting wall that cannot be attacked, an undefeated army reinforcement, a quiet harbor, an impregnable tower, an irresistible weapon, an invincible strength able to discover a refuge in a place no one expects. By this power the unarmed become armed, women fare better than men, and children prove that they easily become stronger than those who practice the arts of war. What wonder if they overcome enemies, when in fact they overcome the world itself... Hope in the Lord changes everything! [31]

2.24.5.en: v Hope carries us forward. It heals us! Do not be anxious and do not despair, lest your hope become vain [32].

2.24.6.en: v No one walks in a good life and is anxious about the future... Does our goodness lean on hope? Yes, but not hope in men, which often vanishes and leaves nothing behind but confusion. Our hope is in God, and it is sure and firm [33].

2.24.7.en: v What does "we are saved by hope" mean? It means that we do not ask for everything for ourselves in this life, and that we have hope also, believing that what God has promised us He will fulfill for us; by this we are saved; for if we lose hope we lose all that we have received...

2.24.8.en: He wishes to say: I ask, were you not subject to countless sins? Were you not in despair? Were you not under sentence?... What then saved you? Hope in God alone, and your confidence in His promises and gifts, for you have nothing else to offer Him.

2.24.9.en: If this is what saved you, let us hold fast to it now also. For He who gave you such great blessings cannot deceive you in the blessings to come. He found you dead and broken and a prisoner and an enemy, and made you a friend and a son and free and righteous and an heir with Him, giving you things so great that no one expected them. After enjoying such gifts generously and lovingly, will He betray you in the things to come?...

2.24.10.en: This way (hope) saved you from the beginning; it is the pledge that you alone brought to the Bridegroom. Let us hold fast to it and keep it, for if you seek anything in this world you lose your goodness by which you became radiant. Therefore the Apostle continues, saying: "But hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man sees, why does he yet hope for?" [34]

2.24.11.en: St. John Chrysostom v Patience directs us toward hope in things to come, and hope directs us toward the reward [35].

2.24.12.en: St. Clement of Alexandria v Why do you rely on yourself and fall? Throw yourself on His arms. Do not be afraid. He will not let you slip. Throw yourself in certainty, and He will catch you and heal you.

2.24.13.en: St. Augustine v Question: How can the soul be fully assured that she is being cleansed from sin?

2.24.14.en: Answer: If a man knows the motive of David, who said: "I hate and abhor lying" (Ps 119:163; lit. iniquity), or knows that he is fulfilling the commandment of the Apostle who said: "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry: for which things' sake the wrath of God comes" and adds to this, as an extension of the sentence against every sin, "on the children of disobedience" (Col 3:5-6), so that he can say: "A froward heart shall depart from me: I will not know a wicked person" (Ps 101:4).

2.24.15.en: Again, a man ascertains that he has such a restraining motive if he bears an emotion with trembling, as the saints do. Therefore David says: "I beheld the transgressors, and was grieved; because they kept not Your word" (Ps 119:158). And the Apostle says: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor 11:29).

2.24.16.en: Now, if according to the truth of the word the soul is above the body (Mt 10:28), and we care for the body, so that we loathe and hate every filthiness and sympathize and grieve from the heart when we see wounds or harm befalling the body, how much more regarding what befalls sinners. For he who loves Christ and loves his brothers suffers for them when he sees their souls wounded as by ravening beasts, and savagely exposed to the attacks of deadly evil. So David says: "My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness. I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long. For my loins are filled with a loathsome disease: and there is no soundness in my flesh" (Ps 38:5-7). The Apostle says: "The sting of death is sin" (1 Cor 15:56).

2.24.17.en: Therefore when a man knows that his soul has come to be in such a state, because of his sins and the sins of others, he is confident that he is being completely cleansed from sin [36].

2.24.18.en: v Question: How must a man turn back from sins (Acts 3:19)?

2.24.19.en: Answer: Through the zeal of David's disposition, who first said: "I acknowledged my sin unto You, and my iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord" (Ps 32:5); then he declared the state of one who learns to work in various ways in the sixth Psalm and in the other Psalms.

2.24.20.en: A man may learn from the Apostle those things that he testified to the Corinthians concerning the sin of others, when he said: "Godly sorrow works repentance to salvation not to be repented of" (2 Cor 7:10). And he adds the signs of that sorrow: "For behold this selfsame thing, that you sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things you have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter" (2 Cor 7:10-11).

2.24.21.en: It is clear from this that it is fitting for us not only to leave sin, and to bear these things on account of sinners, but we must also withdraw from the sinners themselves. David did this plainly when he said: "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity" (Ps 6:8), and the Apostle commanded us: "With such an one no not to eat" (1 Cor 5:11) [37].

2.24.22.en: St. Basil the Great Consider the generations of old, and see:

2.24.23.en: Did any trust in the Lord, and was ashamed?

2.24.24.en: Or did any abide in His fear, and was forsaken?

2.25.0.en: Or whom did He ever call upon, and He despised him? [10]

2.25.1.en: He presents three questions concerning His faithfulness in the generations of old, and with those who trust in Him in the present so that they may enjoy His mercy.

2.25.2.en: Another exercise in the midst of temptations is the study of God's dealings with believers, whether in the Old Testament or the New Testament or throughout history, as in our own life. The God who kept us in the past keeps us in the present and will keep us in the future. The Apostle Paul says: "Who delivered us from so great a death, and does deliver: in whom we trust that He will yet deliver us" (2 Cor 1:10).

2.26.0.en: For the Lord is full of pity and mercy; He forgives sins, and saves in time of affliction. [11]

2.26.1.en: God's attributes here are the foundation upon which man's faith and hope in Him are built.

2.26.2.en: v We have two parents who bore us on earth for misery, and then we die. But we have found two other parents. God is our Father and the Church is our mother, who bore us for eternal life. Let us consider, beloved, whose sons we have become. Let us walk in a manner worthy of such a Father... We have found for ourselves a Father in the heavens; therefore we must pay attention to our conduct while we are on the earth. For he who belongs to such a Father must walk in a way by which he deserves to receive his inheritance [38].

2.26.3.en: St. Augustine v This is the work of God... God created the heavens and the earth and the sea. Great are these works and worthy of His wisdom! But none of these has the power to draw human nature to Him like His mercy and His love for mankind! [39]

2.27.s.en: 3. He who fears the Lord escapes three woes

2.27.0.en: 14 Woe to fearful hearts, and faint hands, and the sinner that goes two ways. 15 Woe to the faint heart, for it believes not, and therefore it shall not be defended. 16 Woe to you that have lost patience, and have forsaken the right ways, and turned aside into crooked ways, 17 and what will you do when the Lord shall visit?

2.27.1.en: He who fears the Lord escapes the three woes that befall him who fails in courage, simplicity of heart and patience.

2.27.2.en: Woe to cowardly hearts and slack hands; and to the sinner who goes two ways [12]. 1. The first woe is for the one with the fainting heart who limps between the two ways, so that he is a member of the people of God and at the same time walks in the pagan ways. 2. The second woe is for him who does not trust in God, and so finds no refuge to take shelter in. 3. The third woe is for him who has no hope; what will he do when the Lord visits him with discipline? Here Ben Sirach refers to David, who chose to fall into the hand of the Lord and not into the hand of man (2 Sam 24).

2.27.3.en: v What does it mean: "Let us draw near with a true heart" (Heb 10:22)? That is, without hypocrisy, for "woe to the fearful heart and the feeble hands" (cf. Sir 2:12). He means: may there be nothing false among us. May we not say one thing and think another, for this is falsehood, and may we not be faint of heart, for this is not the mark of a "true heart" [40].
